At the time I ventured to ask him if he had taken the trouble to consult the provinces who had been parties to the pact of confederation and who naturally would like to have something to say about its alteration. The question was not answered, but the significance of the question evidently sank into the government's mind, because as month after month went by this particular programme of Senate reform became vague and still more vague, and the proposal and method of the reform became in time utterly beyond all understanding. As the election proceeded the in-

The Address-Mr. Meighen
tention to reform some way, any old way at all, was pronounced over and over again by the leader of the government. How far he was followed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) I am in no position to say, 'but I will venture the suggestion-and I ask hon. members to watch the minister-that he never suggested Senate reform to an audience during the whole election. On the doctrine of the solidarity of the government he must have acquiesced in the pledges of his leader, and there was scarcely a platform upon which that leader spoke in the whole campaign which did not resound with his declaration that he was bent upon Senate reform and on one occasion he announced that steps would 'be taken to that end before the next session of parliament. Not only did he so declare, but he said: "Already I have so pledged members who have been appointed to the 'Senate that when they get there they have to vote for Senate reform whether they want to or not. 'Not only have they to vote for Senate reform, but they have pledged themselves to vote for any kind of Senate reform which the government sends up." Thus he described the character of senators who, according to his own admission, he had lately appointed to the upper house. Thus the matter stands until we are greeted in this parliament with the Speech from the Throne, and I look through all its lines in vain; I look through all the perfervid literature that graces its pages, and I cannot see mention of the Senate or of Senate reform. The Minister of the Interior himself looks puzzled. Is it all forgotten?. May I ask, is it forgotten, is it ,afoandoned, or was it in the beginning nothing more or less than a hoax? Was it simply a stage-play by which it was hoped to secure the support Of Labour in this country? In any case the record of the government as regards Senate reform is a very useful object lesson to new and aspiring members of this House as they read, possibly with some enthusiasm, the Speech from the Throne of to-day.
I want to make mention of another topic, and with this I close. In the Speech from the Throne there is a reference to the subject of the tariff. A reading of this paragraph is well worth the time of any hon. member of this House. It is one of the most curiously constructed things I have ever seen. In symmetry it almost resembles the late government

and I use the word "late" intentionally, for hon. members will recall that it was one of the chief boasts of the Prime Minister that his government represented with exactitude the various provinces of our Dominion. We were told with what precise and 14011-14
perfect symmetry the various peoples who compose our population were represented in this government. Now of course the whole picture presents a different spectacle, a spectacle which we find reflected in the promise in the Speech from the Throne to reduce the number of ministers. Well, necessity is the mother of invention and very often it is worth while to make a virtue of necessity. The government apparently intends to carry on with four provinces not represented by a minister and one of them the most populous province in Canada.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. C. ELLIOTT SECONDED BY MR. LIGUORI LACOMBE
speechtext: They are happy provinces.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. C. ELLIOTT SECONDED BY MR. LIGUORI LACOMBE
speechtext:
They are not unhappy. Indeed, if they had their way there would not be any ministers. But they are not allowed to have their way; the country is not allowed to have its way, and that because hon. gentlemen are determined not to interpret the result of the late election by the vote polled but rather in the light of the attractive promises now held out.
On the subject of the tariff one would search in vain for any indication of government policy. We are told that the government is against a general raising of the tariff. How mild and innocent an assertion this is from the authors of the 1919 resolution. What a watering of the strong drink of those times! What a poor and feeble imitation of the courageous spirit which dominated that convention! We have had some changes in the tariff, injurious all of them, changes which hon. gentlemen to my left have described as just a little valise full, and after the valise is filled hon. gentlemen of the government calmly close it and lock it and say they are not in favour of giving anything more. They are not going to raise the tariff; and having said so much they declare that they will appoint a tariff advisory board forthwith. I ask the House to dwell just a moment on the significance of the word "forthwith". Will hon. gentlemen be surprised when I say that the government promised a board two years ago, and promised it in the Speech from the Throne? Then it was called a taxation board. The reason it was not called a tariff board was this, that if they had so named it it would have been an assumption to themselves of a policy announced by the Conservative party in 1912 which they all bitterly opposed. In order therefore to make it look a little different they gave it a drapery and an ensign on which was painted "Board of Taxation." The functions of this board were described by hon. members of the government

The Address-Mr. Meighen

one after another: it was going to investigate tariff matters and modes of taxation. And a motion of the hon. menber for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was even deferred because the Prime Minister declared that the very matter of that motion was to be the object of investigation of this new "board of taxation." Wei], where is the "board of taxation?" I had almost said it had not been appointed, but I really do not know. All I can say is that there has been no result. Indeed, I do not believe it was ever appointed; if it was I should like to be corrected by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). I say I do not believe it has ever been appointed to this day. But do hon. members know that in that year this government passed a vote in the body of the estimates by which they were authorized to make appointments without reference to the Civil Service Commission and they got 830,000 for that purpose? Yet no appointment has so far been made. Not content with that, they came down the next year and asked for another vote to provide them with a tariff advisory board. Hon. gentlemen will note that the colour keeps changing, the appearance is altered, the nomenclature is amended until finally the thing becomes a "tariff board", just a year ago. They got that vote again, but neither taxation board nor tariff board was appointed; and now true to form the administration comes to the House in 1926 and as a new announcement of policy declares to parliament that it will appoint a tariff board and appoint it "forthwith."
What is the intention of the government now? The hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) thinks that this board will help the farmers in the long struggle against drought, and hail and all those precarious circumstances which make their livelihood so difficult; and he hopes that someone will be appointed on that board who like himself has had some experience in countering the winter's blasts and all those other obstacles of nature which obstruct the path of the farmer. I do not see very much connection between a tariff board and those visitations of nature which affect the farmer's crops. However, the Conservative party stands where it has stood all along on this subject; it stands on a policy which would have been the law of Canada for the last thirteen years but that it was defeated by the exertions of hon. gentlemen opposite and their majority at that time in the Senate.
I am going to speak of the verdict of the late election on this subject of the tariff. The hon. member for West Middlesex tells us that the country is very prosperous, and the usual platitudes are poured out to explain 
this prosperity. For example, there is no one, he says, idle in the town of Strathroy. If you look at the government's tale of the national debt and at nothing else you will think, he says, that things are getting better. But we have all heard these words before. True, the prosperity of the country depends upon the prosperity of the working man of every class, and while I am very glad to know that the population of Strathroy is busy I would much rather see the population of Canada busy and I would much rather see the population of Canada increasing. Just a few moments ago I received the employment returns of this country and I find that the employment figure stands for Canada last month at 95.3; that is to say, we have approximately five per cent fewer at work than we had in January 1920, notwithstanding the fact that the system of compilation has improved and the number now returned proportionate to the number employed is greater than it was at that time. Is this a country where the ratio of employment should go down year by year? Has that been the record of the United States since 1920? And we must read even these figures in the light of the fact that in mining, in respect of which this government has no more to do than they have to do with the colour of the clouds, there has been a tremendous increase in employment. If we look at manufacturing alone, 88.1 is the employment figure in December, 1925. It would be less to-day without a doubt, because it is always less in January, whereas for January, 1920, it stood at 100. Well, it might be worse, but surely this is nothing of which to boast; surely we ought to be going ahead in Canada at least from 5 to 10 per cent per year; we should to-day be standing at a figure of from 125 to 135 compared with 100 in 1920. For the past two or three months we have diminished: 98.3, October 1; 97.1, November 1; 95.3, December 1. Hon. gentlemen may say that this is seasonal. Well, I look at their own returns of United States employment, and I read that factory employment in New York state showed a gain of less than one per cent in November as compared with October. Ours on the other hand, goes down: we are 3 below what we were just three months ago. There is a similar report from Massachusetts: persons employed, 235,910 in October compared with 229,946 in September. There is a similar report from Illinois. In Wisconsin, while there has been a slight decrease in number, there has been an increase in the pay rolls. We have a favourable report from every state mentioned in this return, while Canada has gone down by 3.

The Address-Mr. Meigken
Now, I do not say there has been no steadying of conditions in this country; there has been some. Whatever steadying there has been is due, not to any confidence that this government would not like to meddle with our fiscal conditions, but to a confidence that they do not dare bo do so any more. This Dominion is confident that after the result of the last contest this government will not dare to meddle much with tariff matters. Though it may not lack the desire to do so, it certainly will lack the courage. True, hon. gentlemen opposite suggested-because they thought it would be of value to them in the confidence debate; that is the only reason they suggested it-that after all the verdict of the last campaign was for low tariff. Do you see any indication of this conviction in the Speech from the Throne? Do you see any indication of an approach to the goal set in 1919? Do you see any indication of the fulfilment of the words of the Minister of the Interior that the policy of 1924 spelled "the death knell of protection"? Did you hear those words uttered by him even in the course of the campaign? Why, I am told that since October the minister has not gone to a funeral for fear it would remind him of that fatal sentence!
I appeal now to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). Will hon. members hearken to the classic utterances of that hon. gentleman in the debate of but two years ago? Speaking in this House on May 7, 1924, he said:
We are beginning to do slowly what we had endeavoured to do rapidly on three historic occasions and failed-in 1878 and in 1891, unrestricted reciprocity, and in 1911 reciprocity in natural products. We endeavoured to go rapidly, but we were told we were going too quickly and we were defeated in each instance. Now we have been reaching out to the same objective by easy stages-so easy the first two years that our action did not meet with very much approval.
Will he say now as he sits in front of me that they are still marching to the same objective? Are they persevering? Ah! See the lesson of the election on the Minister of Agriculture.	Even he has not misread its
significance. Never will we hear those words from him again,, unless possibly on the eve of another contest-or unless he goes into opposition. If he goes into opposition, all these familiar phrases will return. "The death knell of protection" will have no terrors any more for the Minister of the Interior.
Hon. gentlemen opposite know, and this whole House knows, that the party which I have the honour to lead to-night was sustained on the great issue of protection. Not only were we sustained, but we were sustained throughout almost the length and breadth of 14011-14J
this Dominion; scarcely was there a province where the vote did not indicate that on this great question of fiscal policy the Conservative party was right. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about the vote in the Dominion being for low tariff. I wonder how many hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec were elected upon the tariff policy of this government?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. C. ELLIOTT SECONDED BY MR. LIGUORI LACOMBE
speechtext:
I have spoken in the
province three times for every once his own leader has. It is all very well to say: You cannot count among your supporters the followers of Mr. Patenaude in the province of Quebec. I should like to know: On the question of tariff, on every question debated in the last contest, did the Conservative party of Quebec appeal on any other ground save on the well understood policies of the Conservative party of Canada? They did not. I know full well that there was a difference of opinion as to who should be the leader of the Conservative party; I know that my leadership was not universally acknowledged. Perhaps those who refused to acknowledge it were right. But I want to tell the government that policies are greater than leaders, principles are greater than politicians. Leaders

The Address-Mr. Meighen
may change, but the principles of our party are not only one, they are universally accepted as one throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and nowhere more definitely or clearly than in the province of Quebec.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. C. ELLIOTT SECONDED BY MR. LIGUORI LACOMBE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, (had I observed the time .prior to six o'clock, I should have concluded the few remaining sentences I had to offer before calling it six o'clock. I was in the midst of a reference to the unity of principle upon which the entire Conservative party fought throughout this country during the late election, and had -made some mention of the diversity of views which characterized the professions, of hon. gentlemen opposite who .managed to secure return, a diversity of view equally marked in the late contest as in those which preceded it. I had also stated that none who eared to adhere faithfully to facts would think of ascribing the Liberal victory in the province of Quebec to the tariff policy of that party. I do not want to lay over-emphasis on the character of the campaign conducted by hon. gentlemen opposite and their colleagues and allies, some of the members of the provincial government, in that campaign. Mention indeed is unnecessary. The whole country knows upon what the contest was conducted. The evidence is at hand indisputably. We have it in our possession and it is in the possession of the people of this country. All I can say to hon. gentlemen opposite is this: that a campaign of that character can be overdone. I am proud as a Canadian and proud as a member of the Conservative party to say that there was no counterpart of these methods in evidence in any other part of the country, and I hope there never will be. I counsel hon. gentlemen opposite not to tempt fate too far. I counsel them to have reai consideration for the unity of this country and to see that such consideration is evidenced iby acts, by deeds and by records, rather than having it too often proclaimed in mere empty words.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the acting leader of the House, interjected in the course of my remarks the statement that all candidates in Quebec were elected on the policy of bis government on low tariff. May I refer him to the words of t)he member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) just for the sake of
[Mr. Meighen. i
putting a specific question which I will give him Ojpportunity to answer as I speak, or, if he declines, which I will request him to answer when he takes the floor?
The member for Joliette declared, in language whose clearness was equal to its truth, that he contested his election on a policy of moderate protection. Now I want to ask the leader of the government, is moderate protection now the policy of the Liberal party? I ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture, whom I am delighted to see in our midst, if he conducted his campaign in the province of Saskatchewan on the policy of moderate protection?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. C. ELLIOTT SECONDED BY MR. LIGUORI LACOMBE
speechtext:
The Address-Mr. Meighen
I have now had the advantage of a conversation on the various subjects mentioned in your letter with you and a committee of your members. Consequently my reply will not now need to be so extensive as would otherwise have been necessary.
I made it clear in the conversation, and now repeat, that the policies outlined and elucidated in our interview to-day are the policies of the Liberal-Conservative party irrespective of the source from which it gets its vote either in the House or in the country.
I refer to the following subjects:
1.	The tariff.
2.	The Hudson Bay railway.
5.	Statutory freight rates on grain and flour.
6.	Public ownership of national railways.
7.	The income tax.
9. Transfer of natural resources to the prairie provinces.
^ 10. Trade relations with the United States.
11.	A national coal policy.
With respect to these subjects the stand of the Conservative party has been fully and repeatedly outlined by myself in the House of Commons, and along precisely the same lines elaborated in the country. So far as I know it has never been charged that my attitude as leader on any of these subjects has been equivocal or obscure. In our interview to-day all points on which elucidation was desired were cleared up. I therefore need make no further reference to them now. May I add though that on the subject of the tariff I could not in a few words better define our historic and present policy than to quote what the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King on September 8, in the county of Peel, in the province of Ontario declared to be the policy of the Liberal party, namely-"a tariff which will help to give us what we need in the way of revenue, and, at the same time safeguard industrial development."
As to the others I will take them up separately:
3.	Peace river outlet. Without' doubt there will have to be provided a western outlet for the Peace River territory. It should be provided as soon as possible because until it is that territory cannot develop as so splendid a district should develop because of the very long haul freight rates which now are necessary. At the same time I stated frankly in our interview that I could not undertake an immediate outlay for this purpose. Undoubtedly the cost would run into a very large sum, and we should be in a better position to take care of the responsibilities entailed by railways already constructed before we venture on any new large enterprises. The sooner we are in a position, however, to go on with this the better I will be pleased as we must all have the very greatest sympathy with people who have gone into that district.
4.	Mountain Differential. The principle laid down in the order in council issued by the government of which I was head in 1920, the principle of equalization, was then as definitely and broadly worded as is possible in the defining of any principle. It has not been enlarged, or indeed modified, since. On this principle it is the duty of the railway commission to base their conduct. The function of putting it into effect is theirs, and with the exercise of their function no government should interfere. It is equally reprehensible on the part of a government to pursue the judicial decisions of this tribunal with praise as with blame. If we feel the members of the board are not doing their duty we should take the steps against them which are open to us under the law and not treat them as if they were a political body.
8.	Rural Credits. I am most anxious to see installed at the earliest possible date a sound and sane system of rural credits in Canada. I am opposed to government loans for this purpose and do not think such a

system can over be successfully administered. We should profit by the experience of other countries, and especially o-f the United States. It is our intention to have the operation of their land bank system very carefully studied without delay and it is our confident hope to bring in a measure, certainly at no distant date, based on the general principles found to be successful there. There will necessarily be such modification as may be appropriate to this, a younger country.
12.	Revaluation of Soldier Settlers' Lands. I am strongly in favour of a revaluation scheme, but I must admit I have never myself been able to think of a plan which could be defended on the ground of fairness as applicable to all settlers. The matter will be most sympathetically considered and any plan reasonably defensible on grounds of fairness will be adopted.
13.	Co-operative Marketing. While I have not discussed this subject very fully in the House of Commons, I have on more than one occasion discussed it in the country, and my views are I think well known. The utmost possible assistance will be given to cooperative marketing of farm products of every kind.
14.	Alternative Vote. We are definitely opposed to the alternative vote.
Yours very truly,
I may say I had a letter also from the leader of the Labour party, but I do not think I need detain the House by a perusal of that correspondence. It differs in this respect not by an iota from the correspondence with the leader of the Progressive party. No, our principles have not changed. There are those whose principles have varied and there are those whose practice has never accorded with their principles. There are those who now are moving by slow degrees, so long as they feel they are safe with a majority, away from the stand upon which they secured many of the votes which first of all installed them in office. We stand by the resolution of the 2nd of last June. That resolution embodies those things on which historically the Conservative party has built its faith, those things that have given it the usefulness with which it has served Canada through forty years. That resolution the entire Conservative party stood behind in the late contest, and that resolution we stand behind to-day. Where this government will	move	on the	tariff no oneknows, there is a direction in which I * urge them	at	this time	to go. Whatever may.be said for a tariff commission, there is need of no tariff commission to inform this House,	or	to	inform	any fair-mindedman or woman, that agriculture to-day, in respect of the tariff, labours under a disability, and a disability which it is the duty of this House at once	to	remove.	The agriculture
schedules are not so inter-related with the general tariff structure of our country that we must investigate and await the report of a tariff commission before we attack them. In the market to which agriculture has contributed, which our farmers have been taxed

The Address-Mr. Meighen
to build in that market they should have an advantage comparable with the advantage enjoyed by their competitors in corresponding markets of other lands. They are to-day suffering competition which is doing harm and is discouraging to the agricultural population of this country

comparable with the United States; and that country affects us more than all others together as a competitor; their goods are admitted into this country over less than half the tariff which confronts the products of the Canadian farm on entry to the United States. On what principle of fairness is such a thing continued? Why wait for a tariff commission to remedy an obvious wrong? What other sections of the tariff would be affected by a change of the agricultural schedules? Why, for example, should dairy products, still more, fruit products, still more, vegetable products, produced early on the farms of the United States, come into this Dominion over almost no tariff, satiate the Canadian appetite, destroy the Canadian market, before Canadian goods can come to be consumed? While the American tariff was low, while their cattle schedules were low, their grain schedules low, their mixed farm schedules low, there was reason for keeping the Canadian tariff low also, because our farmers were then on a good plane, on a basis of fair competition with their great competitors across to the south. That was all changed in the fall of 1921. Ever since then the American farmer has monopolized his own market and has had almost equal rights here with the farmers of this country. And not content with that situation hon. members opposite came along and informed the Canadian farmer that in addition he would have to pay a price for the entry of the manufacturer's product into Australia, New Zealand and other parts of the world. This government, which boasts of its trade treaties, not one of which so far has been anything else than a disaster to Canada, -the French treaty, the Italian treaty and the Australian treaty,-introduced a treaty with Australia under which they have admitted into the Canadian market the products of Australian farms, and now of New Zealand farms, in competition with the Canadian farmer over almost no tariff at all, and in most cases over absolutely no tariff. The Minister of Finance will remember, if he will steel himself to do so-he will not do so if he can help it-the speeches he made in parliament telling us that we had not got very much from Australia in the way of farm products, or from New Zealand; so we will let the Canadian farmer in the winter-time compete, practically with no protection against the
Australian and New Zealand farmer, producing at the same time his goods in the summer.
I. have before me a paper published in Vancouver, the Vancouver Province, to which hon. gentlemen have given their imprimatur already this session, and I read the following: New Zealand butter breaks local price.
This is dated January 11, not quite a week
ago.
Over 400,000 pounds were brought in last week and prices slump three cents.
Butter is down from two to three cents a pound. This is the first change that has taken place locally in this commodity for several months, a wholesale basis of 48 cents a pound having been maintained since the fall.
To-day the quotation among wholesale dealers runs from 45 to 46 cents a pounds, top grade.
It then goes on to say that close upon 8,000 boxes, or 448,000 pounds, of butter had landed from New Zealand last week. The closing paragraph states:
An additional shipment from New Zealand is expected inside the next few weeks.
New Zealand was admitted, by order in council of the 26th September, into the benefits of the Australian treaty, and this butter comes into Canada over a duty of one cent a pound. I put this question to the government, whose leader in the city of Kingston declared that industries had to be safeguarded against competition from all parts of the world, even from the country to the south- safeguarded against depreciated currency-I put this question to the government who, through its leader, has expressed such solicitude for the safeguarding of industry and thereby declared that a protective system must continue: How do you justify a protection of one cent a pound in Canada for butter? How do you justify loading on the backs of the farmers of this country the whole cost of a treaty made for the benefit of the manufacturers of Canada? There is one step which can now be taken. It is not only in accord with, but it is one of the great objectives of Conservative policy. I therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton):
That the following words be added to the Address: "We desire respectfully to express regret that the Speech from the Throne gives no indication of policy designed to enlarge the volume of employment in Canada, and particularly to give to the producers of farm products, coal and other primary products the advantage they are, under present world conditions, entitled to enjoy in the markets of this country." .

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted indeed that my first words should be words of agreement with some sentiments expressed by the
The Address-Mr. Lapointe

right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) in the first part of his speech. I join heartily with him in extending to the new members of the House of Commons the most cordial welcome. I may, perhaps, add that if any of them on the other side of the House are not comfortably accommodated, I invite them to come across the floor and we will see to it that they are well looked after. I also agree with him in the congratulations he offered to the mover and the seconder of ithe Address. The hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) comes into the House of Commons with a great reputation which he has won not only at the bar but in other fields, and he has considerably added to it, first, by carrying an important constituency for the Liberal party in the province of Ontario during the recent election-and that was no mean achievement-and, secondly, by his splendid effort of to-day. The hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) is a young and eloquent member of the bar of Montreal, and his talent and industry will be an acquisition to our House of Commons. He replaces in this House a veteran who has represented that constituency for over twenty-eight years, and I earnestly trust that he will have in this parliament as long and honourable a career as his predecessor.
I agree with the right hon. leader of the opposition in the words which he uttered with regard to the honour accorded to Canada at the last Assembly of the League of Nations by the selection of my colleague the leader of the Senate to the presidency of that great body. I have had the honour of attending one of the assemblies of the League of Nations as a representative of Canada, and I know the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), who also, I think, attended one of those assemblies, will agree with me when I say that it is no mean honour to be selected as president of the League of Nations. We knew-and this is the more agreeable to us- that the gentleman who was selected could and did fill the position with dignity and ability.
The leader of the opposition at the opening of his address, offered at least some words of commendation on one of the paragraphs in the Speech from the Throne. I am in favour of reciprocity in courtesy as well as in anything else, and I desire to congratulate my right hon. friend on the somewhat improved tone of his remarks to-day. It is true that "he did not lack the aggressiveness which is always so powerful in eliciting applause from his followers; still, he did not display that spirit of bitterness of which I complained in former years. My right hon. friend was cer-

tainly mostly critical and negative, more industrious in spreading alarm than in giving useful guidance or direction. But on the whole I have no ground for complaint. My right hon. friend is, I think, beginning to be a good loser and he certainly needs to cultivate that spirit in the years to come. He seems to have acquired that quality mentioned by the hon. member for Port William (Mr. Manion) the other day, that is, a sportsmanlike attitude towards defeat, and he does not seem to bear any grudge against the House on account of the vote of Thursday last. If my right hon. friend could only forget that old Tory delusion, that Tories were created by divine right to rule over other people, he would be constructive and he might be helpful in the administraion of public affairs. And having so far commended the right hon. gentleman I suppose I shall be excused if I find it necessary to censure him to some extent. In the first place I fear he displays an extreme indelicacy in formulating and proposing policies for his opponents and in expressing their view's for them. Personally I have never given to the leader of the opposition any mandate to state my own views either on the tariff or on any other question and I desire to be judged rather by what I may say on these matters than by what my right hon. friend represents my views to be.
Another criticism I am constrained to offer has reference to the right hon. gentleman's comments upon the last general election, more particularly as they relate to my own province. May I tell him that his criminations and recriminations in reference to the result of that election and the manner in which the campaign was carried on will receive very little sympathy from the men and women voters in any of the constituencies of Canada who know how the campaign was conducted by himself, or rather by his friends. On this side of the House we have lost some friends as a result of that campaign, but we have the satisfaction of knowing that most of them have been the victims of whispered propaganda and of a lavish expenditure of money, as unscrupulous as it was unprecedented in this country. We have had arrayed against us all the forces of selfishness in Canada.

am sorry that my right hon. friend opposite compels me to refer to the province of Quebec, but I am bound to say this, that that province has emerged from the election greater and prouder than ever she was before. She has proved that it is impossible to make her bend the knee to Baal, or rather to the golden calf, and she has shown, further, that duplicity does not appeal to her. Surely my right hon. friend should not be resentful of Quebec because of that election. Whatever the Liberal electors of that province may think of him, they certainly believe that it was an affront to public morality to keep him outside the province and to compel him in his peregrinations throughout the country merely to hover over that territory,-and that at the behest of what his friends call the Montreal clique. We think in the province of Quebec that my right hon. friend was treated unfairly by those who claim to be his friends in that province, and I do not think that he should resent what has happened there.
All the problems affecting our public life have been discussed in Quebec just as much as they have been discussed in any other province, and some of them to a greater extent even. Even the tariff has been the subject of greater debate in the province of Quebec than elsewhere in Canada. True, the tariff was not the only question discussed there: why should it be? The tariff is only one of the incidents of our national evolution; it is not the whole public of Canada. There are other questions besides the tariff that call for consideration and we have a right to discuss them-nay, it is our bounden duty to do so. And so far as the tariff is concerned I beg to read what Willison's Monthly has to say on the subject. This is a publication which is edited by Sir John Willison, who is by no means a friend of the Liberal party and who is a keen observer of political events in Canada. In its issue of December, 1925, Willison's Monthly at page 250 says:
The British preferential feature of the tariff was discussed more in the province of Quebec during the recent election campaign than in other parts of Canada and in the closing days of the campaign the French language newspapers carried a full-page advertisement under a caption charging that Mackenzie King mani-pule la preference britannique au prejudice de 1*Industrie canadienne.
I repeat, all the features of Canadian life have been discussed not only by myself but by my friends as well in the province of Quebec, as they have been discussed by those who undertake to debate political questions on behalf of the Liberal party. In the presence in this House of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) we have an exemplification of the feeling which prevails in the province of Quebec. Sherbrooke, it will be remembered, was represented in parliament in 1917 and 1921 by an old friend of mine, Mr. McCrea. Mr. McCrea had a weakness, however: he voted with my right hon. friend on the tariff policy; he repudiated the Liberal policy in that respect. And what happened to my dear old friend Frank McCrea? Although the government was quite disposed to allow him to be elected as representative of Sherbrooke, the electors of that constituency declined to nominate Mr. McCrea for the reason that he had voted with my right hon. friend on the tariff question. Is that not a clear case? Instead, the voters of Sherbrooke decided to elect my good friend Mr. Howard, the present member, notwithstanding that it had been charged against him that he had been in favour during the war of a policy which my hon. friends opposite claim was the only question discussed in the province of Quebec in the recent campaign. The present member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) was elected because he approved of the tariff policy of the present government and because he disapproved of the tariff policy of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen).

Every Vote For Sir Henry Drayton In West York is a Vote Against Mackenzie King.
Here is what is said-I do not know whether the tariff is much emphasized in that little paragraph:
The anti-oonfscriptionist of 1917 West York will never vote to send the help of Alexander MacGregor to Hon. W. L. M. King, whose policy refused to send Canadians to the fighting line in time of war, and whose policy does send Canadians to the United States in time of peace.
And in another sentence my right hon. leader is referred to as a cold-blooded traitor. That was to carry the election in West York, to elect my hon. friend who said "hear, hear" a few minutes ago.
Notwithstanding what may be said, Mr. Speaker, the great principle which underlay the Liberal campaign in our province, as well as in the other provinces; the goal which we indicated as the only one worth fighting for, the spirit which we claimed should inspire our acts and policies, was and is that of Canadian unity. It was our aim during the campaign; it was our aim in formulating the contents of the Speech from the Throne, and it is my aim in the remarks which I am making to-night. I believe that the present situation gives to all men in Canada a splendid opportunity to exercise moderation and goodwill, to make a special effort to understand the points of view of our fellow-Canadians in other sections of the country, and to bring all Canada to an understanding which will make our country advance as a unit and not in squads. We shall need in that vision the help and support of all men, and we must learn a lesson of compromise. Our great difficulties in this country come from the fact that the country is divided into four geographical sections separated by natural barriers. It is necessary for all Canadians wherever they live to try to understand the economic interests of the other sections of the country, to learn what the other view-
The Address-Mr. Lapointe

point is, and to reconcile divergent views.
If Canada is to be a great 9 pm. country, the home of a united people, we must recognize the fact that lake Superior is not a barrier between one section and another. Our clear duty is to formulate policies which follow a middle course and can be acceptable to the various interests, whatever part of Canada they represent. Stability is desirable, but it must be stability based upon economic justice to all and upon the necessary requirement of achieving national unity.
During the last general election some of our opponents at least carried on a campaign which, if successful, would make one half of Canada hate the other half. The gist of their arguments in the east, and more especially in my own province, was that this government had sold the east to the west by their actions on tariff and railway matters. I would like, if I had time to do it, to show you some posters which confronted us at every comer in our province. At the same time the right hon. leader of the opposition was stating in the west-as he practically stated this afternoon in his address-that the government had made no concession to western Canada and had "put it over" the Progressives during the last four years.
Hear, 'hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friends applaud, but how can they reconcile this statement with that made in our eastern provinces, namely, that we have sold the east to the west, that we have sacrificed Quebec and Ontario to western interests? One or the other is true ,* surely the two cannot be accurate.
I ask you, Sir, is it a fair task, is it patriotic, to try to. persuade one-half of the country that the other half is unreasonable and wicked?
I say that those who are responsible for such a campaign have sown seed which, if it is not nipped in the bud, will produce a harvest that may work tremendous injury to our people and to our country. The peace and prosperity of the nation will always depend on uniting the minds, the wills and the hands of all Canadians. Our nation is not and cannot be a racial unit. History and the laws of sociology prevent it. It is good that it should be so, because as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) rightly said the other day, to attempt to make it such would denationalize Canada as much as if the American doctrine of the "melting pot" was adopted by this country. We must keep and maintain Canada a political unit and, so far as possible, an economic unit. We must bind the different

parts of it together by common interests. Financial economic and administrative reforms are all desirable, but they will derive their [DOT]highest value from the spirit which inspires them. This spirit must be actuated by justice, kindness, love of truth and confidence in the destiny of our country.
He confesses blindness to stern realities who does not see that refusal to accept*a compromise on the tariff, on the fiscal question, will arouse in Canada an unending agitation. I have already stated in this House, and I state to-day, that I believe in a middle course on the tariff question, with a view of harmonizing to the greatest possible extent the apparently different interests of the various sections of the country. In regard to adherence to the policy of high protection, I say that a country whose area is as large as that of Europe, a country which has a population of only nine millions spread over an immense territory and has natural resources in abundance, cannot enrich herself by erecting a wall around her borders and refusing financial and economic communication with other countries. On the other hand I believe that an industrial system which has prevailed in this country for a large number of years cannot be subjected to an immediate or radical change or revolution without working some injury, and the greatest possible care and precaution must be taken in that respect. Moreover it is obvious that the circumstances) of geography, as I have already stated, have a great influence on the views of the people on fiscal questions. In our huge country we have interests in certain sections which are different from those of other sections. This parliament must act for the whole of Canada and in the interest of all Canadians. Compromise is necessary, and notwithstanding the views of my hon. friends opposite to the contrary, men jn office in Canada must be men of compromise.
The three outsta nding considerations we must have in mind in connection with the tariff question are the interests of revenue, the needs of industry, and the interests of the consumers. The men who will be appointed to the advisory board which we propose will represent various classes and various sections of the country. They will be men outstanding in their respective communities, and it is the hope of the government that their advice-based not only on their own experience but on the data that they will be able to collect-will be of great value in the framing of any legislation concerning the tariff. My views on the tariff are primarily concerned with the interests and the well-

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
being of the whole community, and I will never subscribe to the doctrine which was preached during the recent campaign on many Tory platforms, that the little fellow will be all right when and if the big feHow is all right.
The same spirit has animated the other features of the Speech from the Throne, and they are based on the same principle. My right hon. friend stated this afternoon that the policies set forth in the Speech from the Throne did not mean anything; that they may never be carried out. Well, my right hon. friend no doubt remembers his own experience in that regard, and he speaks from memory. He was Prime Minister of Canada for one session, and one session only,-that which opened in February, 1921. The Speech from the Throne at the opening of that session was the work of my right hon. friend. It is the only Speech from the Throne for which he is wholly responsible. What was the main feature in that Speech? May I read it to you, Sir?
My advisers are convinced of the necessity for revision of the customs tariff. In order to secure the most complete information a committee has conducted an extensive and thorough inquiry-
The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) must remember that it was he who was the investigator.

Oh no, my hon. friend is quite wrong in that. He has forgotten that the American tariff intervened in the meantime, and it was thought that we ought not to go on with it, as was then explained.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is that so? I thought my hon. friend would say he kept his papers as a souvenir.
They are in the office.

However, I will go on with the quotation from the Speech from the Throne in 1921:
-and has secured the views of all parties and interests in every province. The hearings necessary for this purpose have now been completed, and the conclusions founded thereon will be submitted to you in due course. It is the opinion of my advisers that in such revision regard must be had to the necessities of revenue and as well that the principle of protection to Canadian labour and legitimate Canadian industries, including agriculture, which has prevailed for more than forty years in this country must be consistently maintained, but that the customs duties imposed to that end should be no higher than is essential to ensure good standards
of living among our working population and to retain and make possible the normal expansion of the industries in which they find employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

I see my hon. friends
are delighted to hear their policy as contained in the Speech from the Throne in 1921. But it remained there; it never came before the House during that session. Instead of revising the tariff, as my right hon. friend had compelled His Excellency to say the tariff would be revised-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-my right hon. friend proceeded to hold a general election. That policy he submitted to the people instead of to the House. He ran his election on it in 1921; he conducted the election on it in 1925, and I am afraid that Speech from the Throne will serve when the next election comes. We ,do not want to follow my right hon. friend's example in that regard. What is embodied in the Speech from the Throne will be carried out. It is the intention of the government to submit legislation for the carrying out of these policies, and my right hon. friend will 'have the opportunity of voting for or against them.
Now, in the matter of immigration we believe, that in the interests of the country everything possible should be done to secure good immigrants, men who will go on the land. ,We believe this is the opportune time to do that. The time was not opportune during the last few years, but the conditions of business in this country now warrant a Strong policy of immigration. A few days ago the hon. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that we are Maritime-righters; it is true that we place country before party-as all loyal citizens should, and especially all parliamentarians-but he omitted to say that we were of one mind on two main, outstanding and salient points, namely: first, strict adherence to the principles and policies of the Liberal-Conservative party as enunciated time and time again inside and outside this House by the right hon. leader of the opposition; and, a second, unswerving loyalty to the leader of the Conservative party in Canada.
May I add in this respect that the right hon. leader of the opposition is the first leader of any political party in the Dominion that, to my knowledge, has held out anything in the nature of a tangible and specific remedy for the ills that afflict the Maritime provinces? On the other hand, during the last federal contest we had a visit from the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, who came down to the Maritime provinces and asked the people "What are Maritime rights?" or words conveying the same meaning. The Maritime provinces represent a little over a million in population. Of the 29 seats in the three Maritime provinces we returned in the last election 24 members in opposition to the Mackenzie King government-over a four to one shot," in the language of the corridor. On Mr. King's four main points the people decided in the negative, which, as I understand, means against. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) last week endeavoured to promulgate some new theories and some strange doctrine with regard to the reason why people vote at the polls, and expressed the opinion "that you could not accept the popular vote as a verdict." Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that so far as we from the Maritime provinces are concerned, 
none of us arrived here out of sympathy for the Mackenzie King government, or, as the hon. minister suggested, by reason of our personal magnetism or our extreme popularity. We are 'here because of .the expressed will of the people of the Maritime provinces against the government of Mackenzie King. That expression was very pronounced, as you will notice by the number of Maritime righters on this side of the House. The Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, reminds .me of an old saying which went something like this: that it had powder in its cannister but no shot in its locker-that is, a great explosion, a loud noise, but no direct results either good or bad. Almost the opening paragraph of the Speech from the Throne reads as follows:
I congratulate you on the growing prosperity of this favoured land-
And further.
With the improvement of conditions throughout the country.
And still further:
This increased prosperity and advancement have been aided iby the policies of the government.
And so forth. There may be prosperity in some parts of this great Dominion, but in my part of the country there is none. In fact, the condition is the reverse to prosperous. Since 1921 we have lost from the town of Amherst, Cumberland county, over 2,500 of our .population, which is a quarter of the total. We have nearly 1,300 less men employed today than we had in 1921, and the industries of that town are languishing and have been in this condition ever since 1921. What applies to that town applies to almost every other industrial town in the eastern portion of the Dominion, so that portion of those glittering utterances of the so-called Prime Minister does not carry weight or conviction with those who know the facts and realize the stern realities.
May I proceed a step further and refer to a very recent resolution received by me from the general works committee of the Dominion Iron and Steel Corporation at as recent a date as October 6, 1925, which resolution was subsequently endorsed by the Sydney Board of Trade and forwarded to me and, I presume, ito every member of parliament from Nova Scotia. According to this the growing prosperity has not yet invaded that part of the country. There are a lot of recitals with a Jong preamble but I will only read the pertinent parts of the resolution:
Therefore, be it resolved, that the general works committee, representing the men most seriously affected, in meeting assembled call upon the Sydney Board of Trade as being the representative body of the communities' interests to demand of the federal government

The Address-Mr. Smith
that provision for protection be made against the importation of iron and steel from countries with depreciated currency.
Be it further resolved, that the duty against all other countries that have invaded our home market in steel products be sufficiently increased to afford us adequate protection in that we may not have to walk the streets in idleness or be forced to leave our homes to seek employment elsewhere.
Be it resolved, that we consider the steel business in Sydney to be menaced with destruction because and for reasons set forth in this resolution.
Be it further resolved that we are prepared to go before the Sydney Board of Trade and offer concrete cases to show how we are being forced out of employment because we are not sufficiently protected in the matter of steel products.
In December, 1924, just a little over a year ago, Hon. E. H. Armstrong, the then Premier of Nova Scotia, introduced a delegation consisting of representatives of Nova Scotia boards of trade to the government at Ottawa. They asked for a protective tariff on coal and steel sufficient to save those industries in Nova Scotia, and give the workers employed in them a square deal in employment and wages. I would like to quote a few extracts from the memorandum which Mr. Armstrong presented:
The allied coal and steel industries of Nova Scotia have been for some years in a depressed condition. The prospect for the future is that there may be even more serious depression and resultant poverty. The province of Nova Scotia is largely dependent upon these industries which are the main and, in some instances, the sole support of the population in important centres. This will be easily understood when it is considered that from 20,000 to 25,000 men are employed in the mining of coal and its associated industries. And that directly dependent on these there are not less than 100,000 to 125,000 people, or more than one-fifth of the population of the province.
The delegation asked the King government for adequate tariff protection to prevent foreign coal and steel products from flooding Canada's markets; to stabilize and promote the coal and steel industries in Nova Scotia, and to give the working men engaged in them steady and remunerative employment.
It would not appear, Mr. Speaker, that conditions are as rosy in that part of Canada as the so-called government tried to paint them in that picturesque and alluring Speech from the Throne. May I speak further with respect to the coal industry in Cumberland county, which I have the honour to 10 p.m. represent, and also in-the province of Nova Scotia? Our miners have been working on an average one and two days a week for some considerable time. Recently the press of Canada carried headlines about miners in one part of Nova Scotia-not Cumberland county, I am happy to say-resorting to looting and burglarizing. The miners claim that this was done to keep their families from starvation. I do not countenance this violence, but it does seem strange 14011-15J
that miners should be reduced to such straits on account of unemployment when millions of tons of bituminous coal are imported from other countries. With the permission of the House I desire to quote Major Hume Cronyn, K.C., member of the commission which investigated the coal industry in Nova Scotia, whose report, recently presented to the government of Nova Scotia, to my mind sounds a warning note in this matter. Major Cronyn adds to the report an addendum which deals with issues raised at the inquiry, but in respect of which the commission as a whole state they did not feel free to discuss in a report. Major Cronyn states that in his opinion irregularity of employment has been perhaps the greatest cause of distress and discontent among the miners. Further, he goes on to say that the major cause of irregularity of employment is the inability of Nova Scotia coal to compete in the St. Lawrence markets with bituminous coal imported from the United States. He also recommends federal assistance towards the establishment of coking ovens, and a substantial increase in the import duty on all bituminous coal and anthracite screenings. Or in the alternative he proposes a federal bounty on coal shipped from Nova Scotia to Montreal or beyond. Further he says:
It is not -possible to exaggerate the calamitous consequences to Canada should coal mining in Nova Scotia be permitted to decline. If the central provinces are unwilling to sacrifice something of their prosperity on the altar of common citizenship to aid, and perhaps indeed to save the main industry of Nova Scotia, we may witness an estrangement as far as Nova Scotia is concerned of far-reaching consequences.
There must be some national sacrifices, ad Major Cronyn states, if we are to have national unity, and I appeal to all shades of opinion in this House to look these facts squarely in the face and answer whether there is any spirit of unity, any adherence to the spirit or letter of the pact of confederation in a policy which allows one important basic industry of Canada to stagnate, its employees and their families to want, and one of the confederated provinces to languish on account of a glutted Canadian market-a market which was intended for and promised to us under confederation but which is not ours, belonging instead, as it. does to foreign countries on account of our excessive freight rates and insufficient protection. I ask you hon. gentlemen, is that the spirit or the meaning of the union of the provinces, which union was to be a union of patriotism and commercial advantage? The Act of Confederation was not acceptable to us in 1867. We returned but one confederationist from the province of Nova Scotia, the late Right Hon. Sir Charles Tupper,

They do not wish to see any industry which is filling a useful place in the business life of the country put out of operation as a result of any unfair treatment. They have suffered sufficiently themselves in the past from unfair treatment and therefore they have no wish to see the same thing inflicted on others.

No; during those years they were forced to practise thrift, men, women and children were obliged to do without the things they needed because they cost too much. The work of the country was carried on, more lands were cultivated, more of the resources were developed, many new undertakings were entered upon. And so when the more favourable years came along, bringing with them better crops, they were in a position to take advantage of this condition as they could not have done if they had said to themselves, " It will not pay us to do this, because there is no immediate market offering profitable prices; nor will it pay to do the other thing, because we cannot make money just now". After the preparation they had had in those hard years the people of the west gathered some of the fruits of their labour in the good years that ensued in 1924 and 1925 when crops were larger and prices more favourable.
And the reduction in the tariff on implements of agriculture helped to some extent to that end. The restoration of the Crows-nest rates on grain, which meant from 25 to 35 per cent of a benefit from many points, aided considerably also in securing for the farmers more of the fruits of their labour, while the equalization of grain rates east and west encouraged many producers to continue in the hope that better times would come. More efficient marketing |also became the order of the day. According to the best figures available-I am quoting from the Country Gentleman, an American agricultural paper-there was a time when it took on an average four and a half hours of labour to produce a bushel of corn. That was seventy-five years ago: to-day it requires just forty-one minutes to do the same thing. And whereas it took three hours to produce a bushel of wheat at that time it requires today only ten minutes. That and other facts suggest another vital point: the teachings of the agricultural colleges have been lopsided in the direction of production in the past but they have now taken on a new angle; the colleges are now paying more attention to marketing and other phases of rural economics and sociology. The American farmer-and that includes the Canadian-knows how to produce, but what he has not always known in the past is how best to dispose of his products. The effort is being made therefore to secure better marketing facilities and that has contributed to a great extent to the increased prosperity which is felt throughout the Dominion.

The Address-Mr. McLean
Along with better crops and improved marketing facilities there has existed the necessity for wider markets. The farmer of the west does not believe that it pays him better to sell a small quantity of goods at an extremely high price to a limited market than it would pay him to dispose of a larger quantity over a wider area to a greater number of people. Nor does he believe that if you can make a village or a city prosperous it will follow that the country around will become prosperous as well. He does believe that if you can make the agricultural country surrounding a city prosperous the trade of the city itself and of the whole community generally will increase; trade will automatically flow to the city if proper conditions obtain otherwise, and the city itself will naturally prosper if it is properly managed. And so wider markets are needed. The agriculturists of the west rejoiced therefore when about three years ago the embargo on the shipment of cattle to Great Britain for feeding purposes was removed. It is however regrettable that the market to the south of us for Stockers and feeders is not open to us on more advantageous terms. Wherein are we benefited? We are not trading with them at the present time; we have been shut out of their market. If we were able to obtain access there it would be one of the greatest boons conceivable to western agriculture.
